cf.title: Validate GIN posting lists before decoding them

input.subject: Validate GIN posting lists before decoding them

verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection questions the goal: the patches remove out-of-bounds reads on corrupt GIN pages. Two fixable design points remain at level 2, both tied to the backpatch. replication-ondisk-1 asks what redo does with a corrupt posting list in back branches and how a stopped node recovers. maintenance-fit-1 asks for a measurement against unpatched code. Only message #1 is visible, so the judgement rests on thin material.

brief.title: Validate GIN posting lists before decoding them
brief.problem: ginPostingListDecodeAllSegments() and decode_varbyte() do not check segment sizes, varbyte streams or decoded items against the end of the posting list. A corrupt page is read past its end and returns invalid TIDs on release builds or aborts assert builds. Index scans, VACUUM, WAL replay and pageinspect's gin_leafpage_items() reach this code.
brief.proposed_design: Seven patches add bounds checks: decode_varbyte() takes a segment end pointer and becomes a loop, each segment header and its nbytes are checked against the remaining length, and out-of-range or out-of-order items raise an error instead of an Assert(). The output array is sized from len, an unreachable repalloc_array() becomes an Assert(), and pageinspect gets tests.
user_visible_surface: New error when a corrupt GIN posting list is decoded; the thread does not give the message text or SQLSTATE.
WAL replay now stops with an error on a corrupt GIN posting list instead of continuing.
gin_leafpage_items() reports corruption instead of aborting or returning invalid TIDs.
author_claims: Reproduced on release builds of 14 through 18 and on master.
Not a security issue, since normal paths need an already-corrupt page and the crafted-input path is pageinspect.
The loop form of decode_varbyte() shows no measurable performance difference from the nested-if form.
Sizing the array from len does not over-allocate in practice, since a dense list uses about a byte per item.
0001 to 0005 apply back to 14; 0007 is cosmetic and for master only.
brief.thread_state: Only the first message is visible. The author asks reviewers to weigh the WAL replay behaviour change before backpatching, and whether to combine patches.
unclear: The error message, errcode and whether it uses ERRCODE_INDEX_CORRUPTED.
Whether the replay error is ERROR or PANIC on a standby, and how a user recovers from it.
Whether the author measured the cost of the added checks on the decode hot path, beyond comparing the two loop forms.
How amcheck's GIN checks relate to these new checks.
Whether 0006's Assert() is safe in back branches, given the author lists only 0001 to 0005 for backpatching.

prior_attempts.title: Revert refactoring of hex code to src/common/
prior_attempts.quote: As reported by Hans Buschmann, those overflow checks are expensive, and it is possible to see a performance drop in the decoding/encoding of bytea or LOs the longer they are.
prior_attempts.reason:
This is a combined revert of the following commits:
- c3826f8, a refactoring piece that moved the hex decoding code to
src/common/.  This code was cleaned up by aef8948, as it originally
included no overflow checks in the same way as the base64 routines in
src/common/ used by SCRAM, making it unsafe for its purpose.
- aef8948, a more advanced refactoring of the hex encoding/decoding code
to src/common/ that added sanity checks on the result buffer for hex
decoding and encoding.  As reported by Hans Buschmann, those overflow
checks are expensive, and it is possible to see a performance drop in
the decoding/encoding of bytea or LOs the longer they are.  Simple SQLs
working on large bytea values show a clear difference in perf profile.
- ccf4e27, a cleanup made possible by aef8948.

The reverts of all those commits bring back the performance of hex
decoding and encoding back to what it was in ~13.  Fow now and
post-beta3, this is the simplest option.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P13 added overflow checks to hex encoding and decoding in src/common/. This proposal adds bounds checks to GIN posting list decoding, so only the recorded cost of checks in a decode loop carries over.

objections.title: Backpatched replay error can stop standbys and crash recovery after a minor update
objections.failure_scenario: A site updates its standby to the new minor release first, as the release notes advise, while the primary on the old minor keeps writing GIN insert records against a corrupt leaf page. The standby's startup process hits the new error during redo, exits, and loops on the same record at each restart. The site finds out from replication lag alerts and must rebuild the standby.
objections.argument: An error in the startup process ends recovery, so on a standby, or on a primary in crash recovery, it takes the whole node down. Before the patch the same record replayed and the node kept running with one bad index. Message #1 calls the change preferable but leaves the backpatch question open. It does not say what level the redo path raises, or how a user gets past the record without a new base backup or pg_resetwal. Today a REINDEX after promotion or startup fixes a bad GIN index, and that path is lost once the node cannot start.
objections.author_must_show: In back branches, what does redo do with a corrupt posting list, and how does an operator bring a standby or crashed primary back up without restoring from backup?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 names the replay change and asks reviewers to weigh it, but gives no error level and no recovery path for a stopped node. The old behaviour also decoded invalid data, so this is a trade-off to settle before backpatching.

objections.title: Per-byte bounds checks on the GIN decode hot path are not measured against unpatched code
objections.failure_scenario: A user on a minor release runs a full-text or array GIN query that decodes many large posting lists, so decode_varbyte() runs once per item. The new end-pointer test and the loop form add work per byte. The user sees a slower query after the update with no error, and finds out only by comparing before and after.
objections.argument: Message #1 reports no measurable difference between the loop form and the nested-if-with-goto form, but both variants have the checks, so the cost of the checks against unpatched code is not shown. [P13] was reverted because overflow checks added to hex decoding slowed bytea decoding in a visible way, which is the same kind of change: per-byte validation in a decode routine. 0001 to 0005 are meant for 14 and later, where a slowdown found after release is hard to take back.
objections.author_must_show: What is the decode cost of patched versus unpatched master on a scan over large, dense GIN posting lists, such as a common-word full-text search?

precedents.title: Revert refactoring of hex code to src/common/

critic.reasoning: Message #1 compares only two forms that both carry the new checks, so it shows no unpatched baseline. P13 concerns per-byte checks in a decode routine, so it supports asking for a measurement before a backpatch.

refuted.title: No measurement of the added checks against unpatched decoding
refuted.failure_scenario: A user with a large GIN index runs full-text or jsonb queries that decode many posting lists per scan. After a minor release, the per-byte end-pointer checks and per-item order checks make these scans slower. The user sees it only after upgrading a stable branch, where reverting is costly.
refuted.argument: [P13] was a revert of overflow checks added to hex decoding, which caused a measurable slowdown on large values after commit. Here every GIN index scan and VACUUM goes through decode_varbyte(), and the patch adds a check per byte and per item. Message #1 reports no measurable difference between the loop form and the nested-if form, but both forms carry the new checks, so neither is the unpatched baseline. Because 0001 to 0003 target back branches, a regression there would reach users through minor releases.
refuted.author_must_show: How fast are GIN index scans and VACUUM on large multi-segment posting lists with 0001 to 0003 applied, compared with unpatched master?

precedents.title: Revert refactoring of hex code to src/common/

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1, which makes the same point about the missing unpatched baseline and asks for a more concrete measurement.

refuted.title: Backpatched replay error turns a corrupt GIN index into standby outage
refuted.failure_scenario: A site has a standby with a GIN page that is already corrupt. After a minor-release update, redo decodes that posting list, the startup process raises an error, and recovery stops. The standby stays down until it is rebuilt, where before it ran with an index that could be reindexed.
refuted.argument: Message #1 says 0001 to 0003 make corruption during WAL replay raise an error and stop recovery, and it proposes backpatching them to 14. In the startup process any ERROR ends recovery. A user who never asked for the change first sees it as a failed standby after a routine minor update. The author calls the change preferable but leaves the backpatch decision open, and nothing in message #1 describes how a user gets past the failing record.
refuted.author_must_show: In back branches, should the redo path keep its old behaviour (perhaps with a WARNING), and how does a user recover a standby stopped by this error?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-1, which covers the same replay behaviour change and also includes crash recovery on a primary.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: 0001 to 0003 make WAL replay raise an error and stop recovery on a corrupt GIN posting list.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: 0001 changes decode_varbyte() to take a segment end pointer; whether any exported signature changes cannot be seen without the code.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: The patches remove out-of-bounds reads reachable with crafted bytes through pageinspect's gin_leafpage_items(); the author states it is not a security issue.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The author proposes 0001 to 0005 for branches back to 14, including the replay behaviour change.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: New error paths and a rewritten decode_varbyte() in ginpostinglist.c, plus new pageinspect tests with crafted page bytes.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: decode_varbyte() gains an end-pointer check per byte and item checks, and it runs in GIN index scans and VACUUM.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: In back branches, what error level does redo raise on a corrupt posting list: ERROR, PANIC, or a WARNING that keeps the old behaviour?
How does an operator bring back a standby or a crashed primary stopped by this error without restoring from a base backup?
What is the decode cost of patched versus unpatched master on a scan over large, dense GIN posting lists, such as a common-word full-text search?
What are the error message and errcode, and does the error use ERRCODE_INDEX_CORRUPTED?
Is 0006's Assert() meant for back branches, given that 0005 is listed for backpatching and 0006 is not?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows the GIN access method and its redo routines, and who is willing to judge a behaviour change in stable branches.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a redo behaviour change and a decode-path change in every supported branch back to 14. A standby outage or a slowdown found after a minor release is hard to take back.
committability.author_follow_up: No later message is visible. Message #1 raises the replay change for review and offers to combine patches, which suggests willingness to revise.

priority.reason: The fix helps only GIN users with a corrupt page, but it removes out-of-bounds reads and silent invalid TIDs, and adds no new user-visible surface. The patches are small and in one file, but the replay change and the backpatch need a committer who knows GIN, and none has spoken.

provisional_note: The code was not read. The error level in redo, the errcode, which callers reach the new checks during replay, and the real cost of the loop form of decode_varbyte() could not be checked.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: use AV work items infrastructure for GIN pending list's cleanup
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch moves GIN pending list cleanup to an autovacuum work item, requested when the list reaches gin_pending_list_limit. Inserts and updates would then no longer pay for the cleanup.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Masahiko Sawada pointed out that work items run only after an autovacuum run, so the pending list could grow far past gin_pending_list_limit while the same work item is registered again and again. He suggested a soft limit and a hard limit, removal of duplicate work items, and skipping the item if autovacuum already cleaned the index. The author had no time to finish a revised version, so he marked the entry "Returned with feedback" and planned to resubmit.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
So if many insertions happen before executing the autovacuum
work item, we will end up greatly exceeding the threshold
(gin_pending_list_limit) and registering the same work item again and
again.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert the GinMaxItemSize calculation so that we fit 3 tuples per page.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert the GinMaxItemSize calculation so that we fit 3 tuples per page.
Reverted commit(s): Compress GIN posting lists, for smaller index size.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 36a35c55 changed the divisor from 3 to 6, for no apparent reason.
Reducing GinMaxItemSize like that created a dump/reload hazard: loading a
9.3 database to 9.4 might fail with "index row size XXX exceeds maximum 1352
for index ..." error. Revert the change.

While we're at it, make the calculation slightly more accurate. It used to
divide the available space on page by three, then subtract
sizeof(ItemIdData), and finally round down. That's not totally accurate; the
item pointers for the three items are packed tight right after the page
header, but there is alignment padding after the item pointers. Change the
calculation to reflect that, like BTMaxItemSize does. I tested this with
different block sizes on systems with 4- and 8-byte alignment, and the value
after the final MAXALIGN_DOWN was the same with both methods on all
configurations. So this does not make any difference currently, but let's be
tidy.

Also add a comment explaining what the macro does.

This fixes bug #12292 reported by Robert Thaler. Backpatch to 9.4, where the
bug was introduced.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert changes in HOT handling of BRIN indexes
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert changes in HOT handling of BRIN indexes
Reverted commit(s): Ignore BRIN indexes when checking for HOT udpates; Move test for BRIN HOT behavior to stats.sql
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commits 5753d4ee32 and fe60b67250 that modified HOT to
ignore BRIN indexes. The commit message for 5753d4ee32 claims that:

    When determining whether an index update may be skipped by using
    HOT, we can ignore attributes indexed only by BRIN indexes. There
    are no index pointers to individual tuples in BRIN, and the page
    range summary will be updated anyway as it relies on visibility
    info.

This is partially incorrect - it's true BRIN indexes don't point to
individual tuples, so HOT chains are not an issue, but the visibitlity
info is not sufficient to keep the index up to date. This can easily
result in corrupted indexes, as demonstrated in the hackers thread.

This does not mean relaxing the HOT restrictions for BRIN is a lost
cause, but it needs to handle the two aspects (allowing HOT chains and
updating the page range summaries) as separate. But that requires a
major changes, and it's too late for that in the current dev cycle.

precedents_retrieved.title: Iterating on IndexTuple attributes and nbtree page-level dynamic prefix truncation
precedents_retrieved.summary: Patch 0001 adds an API to iterate over index tuple attributes and reuse the offset of the last extracted attribute, so extracting all attributes costs O(n) instead of O(n*n) when attcacheoff cannot be used. Patch 0002 uses this to truncate attribute prefixes dynamically during nbtree binary search within a page, as a first step toward prefix truncation in nbtree.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author's own June 2021 benchmarks showed regressions in multi-column indexes that can use attcacheoff: about 2% for insert and 15% for reindex with both patches. The author said this had to be fixed before commit, but no fixed version appears in the thread. In December 2021 Daniel Gustafsson moved the entry forward and noted that the patch no longer applied and needed a rebase. The visible messages do not show a rebased version or the final decision.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Evidently, this needs improvements in the (likely common) attcacheoff-enabled multi-column case; as I don't think we can reasonably commit a 10+% regression.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow Postgres to pick an unused port to listen
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets `port = 0` make the postmaster bind to any unused TCP port, so colocated instances such as test benches need no port coordination. Clients would read the assigned port from postmaster.pid.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane called reading the port from postmaster.pid a poor interface and preferred that test frameworks choose the port. Aleksander Alekseev argued the approach is unreliable for the stated problem. Reviewers then asked for the port to be reported through a separate file or a pg_ctl command, which would also fit future per-interface ports. The author posted no revised patch after May, so the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I think either a specific pg_ctl command to return the port like Greg had initially mentioned or simply a separate file to store the port numbers would be ideal.

precedents_retrieved.title: Pageinspect - add functions on GIN and GiST indexes from gevel
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Alexander Korotkov, Tomas Vondra, Ashutosh Sharma, Peter Eisentraut
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch moves the gevel module's functions for GiST, SP-GiST and GIN indexes into pageinspect, with tests and docs. The functions show whole-index statistics, print the tree and its stored objects, and estimate GIN value counts and query matches.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers said the functions read the whole index, while pageinspect inspects single pages, so the code belongs in a new extension or should be rewritten as page-level functions. Peter Eisentraut also found that the patch no longer compiled and that the stats functions returned one formatted text value where they should return a row with columns. The author planned a new contrib module but posted no new version, and the entry was returned with feedback after three weeks of waiting on the author.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The proposed patch uses a very different approach, reading the whole index,
not individual pages. Why should it be part of pageinspect?

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow pageinspect's bt_page_stats function to return a set of rows instead of a single row
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch first changed pageinspect's bt_page_stats to return a set of rows covering a range of B-Tree pages, with a pageinspect version bump to 1.11. After review it added a separate function, bt_multi_page_stats, which takes an index, a starting block number and a block count.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane listed open issues before the patch could be committed: no documentation update, no simple way to ask for all remaining pages (a count one too large raises an error), and a regression test that depends on tuple layout. He then showed the test fails on a 32-bit machine. The author did not address this feedback, and Michael Paquier marked the entry Returned with feedback after four weeks of inactivity.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This feedback has not been addressed and the thread is idle four
weeks, so I have marked this CF entry as RwF.

precedents_retrieved.title: GIN fillfactor
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a fillfactor storage parameter to GIN indexes so that index build leaves free space on pages, and apply it to the page split ratio in dataPlaceToPageLeaf. The default was debated between 100, which matches the packed 9.4 indexes, and 90.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No benchmark showed that the option improves performance. Heikki Linnakangas tested random updates and found that GIN indexes do not bloat after build, because posting tree pages already keep some free space, so he concluded the option is not useful in practice. Alexander Korotkov showed one case with bloat but agreed it was probably not worth it without real use cases.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Based on this, I think we should just drop this patch. It's not useful in
practice.

precedents_retrieved.title: amcheck verification for GiST
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a GiST verification function to contrib/amcheck that checks parent/child key consistency and that all leaf pages are at the same depth. Later versions hold buffer locks on parent and child pages together and take only an AccessShareLock on the relation.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Peter Geoghegan questioned whether the checks are safe under an AccessShareLock, since Heikki's v6 had used a ShareLock. He doubted that the parent re-find logic copied from gistfinishsplit() applies here and asked how concurrent page deletion could affect it. Andrey Borodin did not answer these questions for about two months, so Michael Paquier returned the entry with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: My main concern now is the heavyweight lock strength needed by the new function.

precedents_retrieved.title: Remove page-read callback from XLogReaderState
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch removes the page-read callback (and later the open and close segment callbacks) from XLogReaderState. XLogReadRecord becomes a state machine that returns XLREAD_NEED_DATA, and the caller then loads WAL pages itself.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Thomas Munro committed a squashed version in April 2021, and it was later reverted. The author's note mentions a possible defect on one platform but does not give the cause. In September 2021 Thomas Munro pointed the author to a message from Andres Freund that the author had not seen and had not yet answered, and the entry was then returned with feedback. The visible messages do not show the content of that message or the exact reason for the revert.

roaster_notes.note: No earlier attempt at hardening GIN posting list decoding appears in the precedent list. The one row found is related only through its performance reason.

The user-facing surface is small: no syntax, GUC, catalog or dump change. Only the backpatched WAL replay behaviour raises a compatibility concern. The error text and errcode are not shown, so I could not check them against existing index corruption reporting.
The patch changes no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog, protocol or exported API. Only the replay behaviour change touches this angle.

The proposal adds no privilege or exposure; it removes out-of-bounds reads on corrupt GIN pages. A non-superuser cannot write crafted page bytes, and gin_leafpage_items() is superuser-only, so the author's 'not a security issue' claim holds from this angle. The standby-stops-on-error change belongs to other angles; [P13] concerns hot-path cost, not security.

The fit with core is sound. This is validation inside an existing core routine, adds no new API or dependency, and needs little ongoing maintenance. The only maintenance-angle concern is the unmeasured cost on the decode path.

No existing feature does this job. amcheck checks an index only when someone runs it, so it cannot stop an index scan, VACUUM or WAL replay from decoding a corrupt posting list. Bounds checks inside the decoder are the only place this protection can live, and no hook or extension could add them.

This is a bug fix: decoding a corrupt GIN posting list reads past the page end and returns invalid TIDs, reproduced on 14 through master. Any GIN user with a damaged page benefits, the cost falls mostly on the decode path, and a committer would not ask for demand evidence before fixing an out-of-bounds read. The thread shows no field reports, but that does not weaken the case for a fix. The WAL replay change and the cost on the decode path belong to other angles.
